Circles Through Orthocenter

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture to explore: circles drawn on the sides of a triangle meet the sides in six points, and those six points always lie on one circle. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the blue corners A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names and the hint that explains the circle.

Drag a corner, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

This picture came from Problem 1 of the 2008 International Mathematics Olympiad. At first the six points look as if they have no reason to line up on one circle — until you notice where the circle's centre must be.

Three circles through H

Drop the three altitudes of triangle ABC; they meet at the orthocenter H. Let Ma, Mb, Mc be the midpoints of BC, CA, AB. The circle centred at Ma through H cuts the line BC at A1 and A2; its radius is ra = MaH, so the two crossings sit that far either side of Ma. The other two circles give B1, B2 and C1, C2 in the same way.

The circle is centred at O

Let O be the circumcenter of ABC and sa = OMa. Because O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, OMa is perpendicular to BC, so Pythagoras gives OA12 = sa2 + ra2 — the same for A2. The page compares powers of the vertices to show (a/2)2 − ra2 = (b/2)2 − rb2 and, since (a/2)2 + sa2 = R2, that ra2 + sa2 = rb2 + sb2 = rc2 + sc2. All six points are therefore concyclic about O. The logic test checked both equations and the six equal distances on more than four thousand triangles, to within 0.00001 board units.

Red herrings and a small quirk

The page notes that "acute-angled" is a red herring: the six points are concyclic for any non-degenerate triangle, and even the altitudes can be replaced by other concurrent lines. H is the radical center of the three circles and each altitude is a radical axis. In a right triangle H is a corner, the three chosen crossings can coincide, and the applet's own three-point circle has no centre; this port draws the proved circle centred at O instead, so the picture still tells the truth.

Tick Hint and drag one corner far to a side: the dashed circumcircle, the segments joining the midpoints and the highlighted dots show the radical axes lining up with the altitudes.
